## Introduction

In this overview, we start from the report you just
updated. We work out what a colleague would need to rerun it, then see
how a GitHub release and an archived Zenodo record keep those materials
together and citable. We finish with what to do when the data cannot be
shared.

**Question for the room.** Think of the report you just rendered. What would a colleague need to rerun it exactly and get the same numbers?

Answers below:

## Decide what to archive {#decide-what-to-archive}

Each part of `workspace/report.html` points to files a colleague would need.

| In your report | Files that support it | Where they go |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Methods and results | `.here`, `workspace/report.qmd`, and `outputs/health-wellbeing/meta-summary.csv` | Track the project-root marker and report source. Attach the summary and the rendered HTML. |
| Pipeline script MD5, variance estimator, and interval method | `workspace/_targets.R`, plus the support and preparation scripts it relies on | Track. |
| Upstream snapshot, raw and selected input MD5s, and inclusion rule | The data source and upstream notice in `data/raw/`, and the dataset metadata | Track. Attach any FAIR assessment record. |
| Dataset and predictive model pin versions | `analysis-data-version.txt`, `dataset-versions.csv`, `predictive-model-version.txt`, and the pins | Attach the version files. Attach the pins if permitted and needed to preserve the exact stored versions. |
| R and *meta* versions | `renv.lock`, the Dockerfile or image reference, and the session record | Track the lockfile and Dockerfile. Attach the session record. |

The files can be managed with version control using `git`.

## Releases on GitHub {#archiving-releases}

A Git commit identifies a repository revision. A
GitHub release gives a tagged revision a name and a place for release
notes and attached files. 

An archiving service such as Zenodo can store a copy of selected files
and issue a Digital Object Identifier (DOI). An archive makes the cited files available under the
access conditions of that record [@zenodo-reserve-doi].

One release ties your pipeline, report source, lockfile, and metadata
together at one tagged revision. A reader can then retrieve that exact
combination rather than the repository's latest state. In the workshop
repository, preparing a release follows the steps we have used
throughout the session:

1.  Record the changes in the [`CHANGELOG.md`](https://jbris.github.io/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/CHANGELOG.html) and commit that entry. 
2.  Tag the commit and publish a release with notes on the [releases
    page](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/releases).
3.  Publishing the release builds and pushes the RStudio and Binder Docker images.
4. With Zenodo integration enabled for the repository, Zenodo also archives the tagged files.

## Inspect a Zenodo record

[Workshop
archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24342489) · [GitHub
releases](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/releases)

Open the workshop's Zenodo record [@workshop-zenodo]. Find the creators, access conditions,
the ZIP of the archived revision, and the list of versions. The concept
DOI, `10.5281/zenodo.24342489`, represents all versions and always
resolves to the latest one. 

The workshop has three connected locations:

| Resource | Role |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| [Workshop website](https://jbris.github.io/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/) | Read the published workshop materials. |
| [GitHub repository](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r) | Find the source files, history, and releases used to publish the site. |
| [Zenodo archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24342489) | Find and download the archived releases. |

Each version's related identifier points to the GitHub release tag it
archives. 

As a follow-up, assess the workshop's software record using the concept
DOI. Select the FAIR for Research Software metrics in *rfair*. The FAIR
lesson used research-data metrics for the HealthWellbeing snapshot
[@rfair].

```{r health-fair-software-archive, eval = FALSE}
archive <- rfair::assess_fair(
  "https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24342489",
  metric_version = "0.7_software", timeout = 10, max_time = 60
)
archive
```

## Supplementary: When the data cannot be shared

Open science can include restricted-access data:
you can share the methods, code, metadata, and access conditions while
restricting the original observations.

Synthetic data generated with *synthpop* can help others test whether a
workflow runs. It does not let them verify findings computed from
data that cannot be accessed, and it does not guarantee privacy. The [supplementary synthetic data exercise](10_synthetic_data.qmd) works through an example after the workshop.

## After the workshop: archive your own releases {#zenodo-github-integration}

To archive releases of your own repository, follow Zenodo's [Enable a
repository
guide](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/github/enable-repository/):

1.  Connect your GitHub account to Zenodo if it is not already linked.
2.  In Zenodo's profile menu, select **GitHub**.
3.  Select **Sync now** to refresh the list of repositories.
4.  Find the repository you maintain and enable its slider.
5.  Refresh the page and check that the repository is enabled.

Once connected, publishing a new GitHub release triggers automatic
archiving in Zenodo. Inspect the resulting version record, its DOI,
metadata, and downloadable files after each release. The **Sync now**
control refreshes the repository list; published releases are the events
that create new archives.
